title: When the Smile Turns
premise: Beatrix Amberdale hosts a dead-of-night radio show from a decommissioned station where the founders once conducted a ritual to bind the town's dead to the airwaves. When her sleep recordings reveal a second voice answering questions she never asked aloud, she learns the ritual was left unfinished and the dead are choosing her as its completion. As the founders' descendants close in to claim the power for themselves, Beatrix must decide whether justice belongs to the living or the wronged dead, finishing the ritual on her own terms and dissolving the station's hold forever.
about_author: August Whitlock is the pen name of a former overnight radio producer who spent years in empty studios and swears at least one of them talked back. They write horror about ordinary people who inherit obligations they never agreed to.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. She runs her lonely call-in show, counting doors and keeping lights on, until a caller describes his own funeral from last week in perfect detail. The emotional beat is quiet dread: the comfort of routine curdling into the certainty that something has noticed her.

chapters.title: The Sleep Tapes
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Reviewing her sleep recordings, she hears herself asking questions and a second voice answering in a register no human throat makes. She begins transcribing the answers, learning fragments of the founders' ritual. Beat: fascination overtaking fear.

chapters.title: Founders' Frequency
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV, with an intercut of descendant Marcus Hale's. She researches the station's 1930s origins and finds a sealed broadcast log; meanwhile Marcus realizes someone is listening to the old frequency again. Beat: two hunters circling the same secret.

chapters.title: The Counted Doors
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. The building's geometry betrays her—doors she counted at twelve now number thirteen, and hallways loop back on themselves. A dead caller warns her that the station is 'waking up.' Beat: claustrophobia and the loss of safe ground.

chapters.title: What the Dead Want
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Through the sleep voice, she learns the dead were bound without consent, their grievances unresolved for ninety years. The voice asks her to be their advocate. Beat: reluctant empathy; horror reframed as injustice.

chapters.title: Descendants
chapters.summary: Marcus Hale's POV. He and the other heirs arrive in town, armed with the founders' notes and a plan to seize the unfinished ritual's power before Beatrix can interfere. Beat: cold ambition; the reader sees how power corrupts the living faster than the dead.

chapters.title: Interference
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The Hales jam the frequency and cut the station's power, but the dead route through every speaker in town instead. Beatrix realizes they don't need the transmitter—they need her. Beat: escalation and betrayal of the rules she trusted.

chapters.title: The Thirteenth Door
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Guided by the sleep voice, she descends beneath the studio to the founders' original chamber, where the ritual's missing final step is carved into the floor—and where Marcus waits. Beat: confrontation; the choice between hiding and acting crystallizes.

chapters.title: Going Live
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. In the chamber, Marcus attempts to complete the ritual for himself and is unmade by the accumulated grievances he refuses to hear. Beatrix speaks the closing words not as a master but as a witness, giving each dead voice its hearing. Beat: climax—justice outside the law, paid in attention rather than blood.

chapters.title: Sign-Off
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. The station goes silent, the thirteenth door closes, and the callers stop—but one last voicemail thanks her by name. She leaves the lights off for the first time. Beat: bittersweet resolution; memory honored, power relinquished, invisibility finally chosen rather than imposed.
